title: Doubt whether one is in grace is a defect to fight, not a virtue to foster
source_text: XXXI. Nec etiam, quod inde consequens est, inter eos quaeritur, Num dubitatio illa qua quis haesitat & fluctuat, super eo num sit in Dei gratia, & an Deum habeat propitium atque benevolum, sit aliquid in fideli laudandum & fovendum, An vero defectus & tentatio quaedam contra quam ipsi luctandum est, & ex qua modis omnibus niti debet ut se expediat: Istud enim audivimus modo fatentem Stapletonum, nec dissentiunt reliqui Scholae Romanae Theologi, qui facile concedunt fideles esse nimium, ut loquuntur, scrupulosos, si non arguente eos conscientia gravis alicujus peccati, cujus poenitentiam non egerint, de propria gratia dubitent.
pass_a_gloss: Nor also, which is consequent from that, is it asked among them whether that doubt by which someone hesitates and fluctuates over whether he is in God’s grace, and whether he has God propitious and benevolent, is something in the faithful to be praised and fostered, or rather a defect and a certain temptation against which he himself must wrestle, and from which he ought to strive by all means to free himself: for we have just now heard Stapleton confessing that, nor do the remaining theologians of the Roman School dissent, who easily concede that the faithful are excessively, as they say, scrupulous, if without their conscience accusing them of some grave sin for which they have not done penance they doubt concerning their own grace.
pass_b_english: Roman doctors do not praise lingering doubt about one’s gracious standing.
With Stapleton they treat such hesitation as a defect and temptation to be fought—especially when no unrepented grave sin accuses the conscience.

choices.why: Roman technical charge of excess anxiety.
